title: Go AI Agent Framework With Retries, Budgets and Human Approval
summary:
One of my team's main projects has an AI-heavy backend written in Go. I work mostly in Python, where agent frameworks are mature, so I know what the Go side was missing: an agent that's a normal value inside the service, not a Python process reached over a queue. The loop itself takes an afternoon. Deciding what happens at each place it can break is what became Golem, an open-source Go AI agent framework.

This post is about that second part: bad tool calls, provider errors, loops, cost and human sign-off, and where each one lands in a run. It also covers how Golem compares with the other Go options and when you should pick something else. It describes v1.2.0, released on 16 November 2026.

What breaks once the agent loop is running?

The loop is short. The model reads a conversation, asks for a tool, you run it, you feed the result back and repeat until the model answers. Each step then fails in its own way:

  • The provider returns a 429 or a 503 halfway through a run.
  • The model calls a tool with arguments that don't match your schema.
  • The model returns JSON that is almost the shape you asked for.
  • The model asks for the same tool call again and again.
  • A tool needs a person to approve it before anything irreversible happens.
  • A run dies on turn six and you lose the first five turns.

Python has good answers to several of these. Pydantic AI showed that an agent can have typed dependencies and validated output, and I used it as a reference. But copying Python mechanisms into Go would have given me something un-Go-like: decorators are awkward, runtime validation hides what the compiler could check, and exceptions as control flow don't suit a language that returns errors. So the question I started from was what an agent should look like if you begin with Go's strengths.

What is Golem?

Golem is an open-source Go library for building agents. The repository started on 16 August 2026, and v1.0.0 on 25 October 2026 froze the API under a rule written down in ADR 0041: semantic versioning, additive changes only below v2, checked by an API diff against the previous tag.

The short version:

  • Agents are generic: Agent[Deps, Output]. Dependencies and the final output are real types.
  • The module has no dependencies outside the standard library, and needs Go 1.26 or newer.
  • Adapters cover OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and local models through Ollama or LM Studio.
  • An MCP client works over stdio and streamable HTTP, and an MCP server exposes one agent as a tool.
  • Retries, fallback models, self-correction, usage limits, loop detection, streaming and run events are built in.
  • A deterministic fake model lets you test agents offline.
  • It ships with 39 guides, every example runs offline, and statement coverage is 81.6%. 
go get github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem

The layering is plain. Your service owns the dependencies, the core owns the run, and everything that touches the outside world sits behind a small interface.

Why build agents in Go at all?

Agent work is mostly waiting on a network, so it's fair to ask whether the language matters. I think it does once the agent leaves the notebook. An agent service holds many conversations at once, calls tools concurrently, streams tokens to clients and has to shut down cleanly. Goroutines, context.Context and a single static binary fit that shape. A deployed agent can be one small container image with no interpreter, no virtualenv and no dependency tree to audit.

The compiler is the second reason. When a tool depends on a database handle and a tenant ID, I want the compiler to tell me if I pass the wrong one. In Golem that's a type parameter, not a convention.

What does a first agent look like?

This is the smallest working agent, from the README:

client, err := openai.New(openai.Config{
    APIKey: os.Getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
    Model:  "gpt-4o-mini",
})
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

agent, err := golem.New[struct{}, string](client,
    golem.DecodeFunc[string](func(_ context.Context, r model.Response) (string, error) {
        return r.Message.Content, nil
    }),
)
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

result, err := agent.Run(context.Background(), golem.RunContext[struct{}]{}, "Why is Go ideal for AI agents?")
fmt.Println(result.Output)
fmt.Printf("Tokens: %d input, %d output\n", result.Usage.InputTokens, result.Usage.OutputTokens)

You build the agent once with golem.New and run it many times. It needs a model and an output decoder, and the decoder is the line where untrusted model text becomes a value your program is willing to use. Everything else is an option function. The result carries the typed output, the full normalized conversation and cumulative token usage.

How do typed tools and dependencies work?

Most agent bugs I've seen live in tools. A tool needs a database, an HTTP client or a user identity, and frameworks often solve that with globals or closures, which makes tools hard to test. In Golem a tool is a typed value, and its Exec function receives the run's dependency value directly:

type Database struct {
    Users map[int]string
}

getUser := tool.MustNew(tool.Tool[Database]{
    Name:        "get_user",
    Description: "Look up a user name by their ID.",
    Schema: json.RawMessage(`{
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"id": {"type": "integer"}},
        "required": ["id"]
    }`),
    Exec: func(ctx context.Context, db Database, args json.RawMessage) (tool.Result, error) {
        var input struct {
            ID int `json:"id"`
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(args, &input); err != nil {
            return tool.Result{}, err
        }
        name, ok := db.Users[input.ID]
        if !ok {
            return tool.Text("User not found"), nil
        }
        return tool.Text(name), nil
    },
})

agent, err := golem.New[Database, string](client, decoder,
    golem.WithTools[Database, string](getUser),
)

result, err := agent.Run(ctx, golem.RunContext[Database]{Deps: Database{Users: map[int]string{42: "Alice"}}}, "Who is user 42?")

The schema is written by hand and the arguments arrive as raw JSON. That's deliberate. Arguments are untrusted model output, and I'd rather you see the validation than have reflection do it somewhere you can't read. It costs a few more lines per tool, and in return a tool's behavior is visible in the file where it's defined.

What happens when a run goes wrong?

A Golem run is a transparent loop, and each failure has a named place to land.

How does an agent correct bad output?

When the model returns bad output or bad tool arguments, the cheapest fix is often to say what was wrong and ask again. A decoder or tool does that by returning an error that wraps *model.ModelRetry:

if input.N <= 0 {
    return "", &model.ModelRetry{Err: fmt.Errorf("n must be positive, got %d", input.N)}
}

The run feeds that message back to the model. Self-correction is opt-in, with separate budgets from WithOutputRetries and WithToolRetries, so a model can't argue with your validator forever. With no budget, the same error fails the run at a named stage with its cause intact. A failure the model should simply see, like a missing file, is &tool.Failed{Reason}: the model gets the reason as a tool result and no retry budget is spent.

How do you survive provider errors?

Transient provider errors (408, 429, 5xx and transport faults) are retried with WithMaxAttempts. The default is one attempt, so retries are opt-in. Backoff starts at 500 ms, doubles and caps at 30 seconds unless you supply your own. Tool and decode failures are never retried by this mechanism, since they aren't transport problems.

When retrying isn't enough, model.NewFallback(primary, backup) tries models in order. For streams there's one rule: a fallback only happens before the first fragment is forwarded, because after the caller has seen output, switching models would replay it.

How do you stop a runaway agent?

Two limits cover it. golem.UsageLimit bounds input, output and total tokens, model requests and tool calls, and a dollar cost if you supply a price table with WithPrice. Token counts come from the provider's reported usage, so a token limit only trips when the provider reports usage, while requests and tool calls are counted by the run itself. Pricing is yours to supply, because I don't want to ship a table that goes stale between releases, and the library says plainly that the cost estimate is only as good as your rates and isn't a billing guarantee.

The second limit is loop detection, added in v1.2.0 (ADR 0051). WithLoopDetection(maxRepeats) counts calls to the same tool with canonically equal arguments across the whole run, and fails the run before the offending call executes. That ordering is the point: a model that polls a tool can't repeat a side effect while you wait for the check. WithLoopPolicy adds checks for repeated results, alternating A-B calls and repeated final text, with a choice between stopping the run and nudging the model.

Oversized tool output is the quieter cost. WithToolOutputLimit caps a tool result before it enters the conversation, keeps the head and tail, and appends a marker with the original size (ADR 0050).

What do you keep when a run fails?

When a run fails on turn six, you still want turns one to five. Golem attaches them to the error as RunError.Partial: the conversation through the last completed turn, the usage so far and the counts of requests and tool executions. Pass Partial.Messages to RunWithHistory to resume instead of starting over, which matters when the run has already spent real money.

How does an agent wait for a person?

Some tools shouldn't run without sign-off: deleting files, moving money, sending email. A tool defers by returning an error wrapping *tool.Deferred, of kind tool.DeferApproval or tool.DeferExternal. The other tool calls in that batch execute, and Run returns successfully with Result.Pending listing what's waiting. No further model call happens.

You resume with RunWithDeferredResults, passing the paused conversation and a decision for each pending call. Approved calls run, denied calls tell the model it was denied, and external results are inserted as given. Because a pause is a returned value, you can store it, show it in a UI and resume it hours later from another process. The reasoning behind that boundary is in the case for keeping meaningful actions with people.

Can a Go agent use MCP?

The Model Context Protocol is now the usual way to expose tools to agents, so Golem includes a client. mcp.NewStdio starts a server as a subprocess, mcp.NewHTTP connects to a remote endpoint, and mcp.AsTools turns the server's tool list into ordinary tool.Tool values with the server's own schema. A server error flagged as isError comes back as a correctable ModelRetry, and protocol or transport failures fail the run instead of being quietly corrected.

The guide says one thing I agree with: don't reach for MCP when a typed Go tool is one function away. A subprocess speaking JSON-RPC has more moving parts than a function call.

How do you test an agent without a model?

Agent tests are usually flaky (a real provider) or meaningless (mocked HTTP). Golem ships testmodel, a scripted in-memory model that plays back the responses you queue and records the exact request the agent sent:

client := testmodel.New().Respond(
    model.Response{Message: model.Message{Role: model.RoleAssistant, Content: "pong"}},
)
agent, _ := golem.New[struct{}, string](client, decoder)
result, err := agent.Run(context.Background(), golem.RunContext[struct{}]{}, "ping")

You can assert on the normalized request, the ordered messages in Result.Messages and which stage failed, with no network, keys or sleeps. The repository's CI runs its suite with the race detector, plus a fuzz target on the message JSON format.

How does it compare with other Go agent frameworks?

I compared Golem with the three other Go options I'd look at: langchaingo, Eino and Genkit for Go. I read each repository's source tree and go.mod on 27 November 2026. Dependency counts are the non-indirect lines in the require block, so they're approximate, and frameworks move fast, so check upstream before you depend on a detail.

Golem langchaingo Eino Genkit (Go)
Direct dependencies 0 About 60 About 10 About 40
License MIT MIT Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0
MCP client In the core module Not in the repository Separate eino-ext module Plugin in the repository, client and server
Pause for human approval tool.Deferred, resumable Not found Interrupt and resume in adk Tool approval middleware
Retry and model fallback Built into the run Not found Retry and failover in adk Retry and fallback middleware
Design centre One explicit agent loop with typed dependencies LangChain-style chains and agents Graph and workflow composition Flows with OpenTelemetry tracing

Two things stand out. Golem is the only one with no dependencies outside the standard library, and the only one where a tool receives a typed dependency value for the run. I haven't found an equivalent of RunContext[Deps] in the others, but I haven't audited every API, so read that as what I found, not a proof.

The other half is that Golem is not alone on the guardrails. Genkit's Go module ships MCP, retry, fallback and tool approval as plugins and middleware, and Eino's adk package has retry, failover and interrupt-and-resume. Only langchaingo lacks them in the repositories I read. The Golem README understated Genkit on this.

The others are ahead in other places. Eino's graph model is more expressive than Golem's linear loop for branching, parallel and multi-agent pipelines, and it has more community components. langchaingo covers more providers and vector stores. Genkit has first-party Google tooling and tight Gemini integration. What Golem offers is a smaller surface: one runtime for a single agent inside a service, with the controls in the core module instead of in add-on packages.

When should you pick something else?

Pick Golem if you want agents inside a Go service, typed dependencies, a module with nothing else to audit and tests that run offline. Pick something else if your agent is mostly prompt experimentation, if you need a graph engine for complicated multi-agent pipelines, or if you need a large catalog of prebuilt integrations today. Python is still ahead on that last one, and I won't pretend otherwise. Golem also has no evaluation harness and no durable workflow engine, and v1.0.0 lists both as non-goals.

Herbie, a self-hosted chat and workflow app I built, runs its Go backend on Golem. I don't have production numbers to publish yet, so everything above is design reasoning plus what the repository's tests and examples show.

The documentation site has a guide for each feature, and examples/ has runnable programs for nearly all of them, several with no API key.

  • Project page: the Golem overview and capability matrix
  • Repository: github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem
  • Docs: abubakarsiddik31.github.io/golem
  • API reference: pkg.go.dev/github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem

Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you try it and something feels un-Go-like, I want to hear about it.

Frequently asked questions

What is Golem?
Golem is an open-source AI agent framework for Go. It provides typed agents, tools with dependency injection, structured output, MCP support, and controls like retries, usage limits, loop detection and human approval.

Does Golem have external dependencies?
No. It uses only the Go standard library.

Which LLM providers does it support?
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and local models through Ollama, LM Studio or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Can I test agents without calling an API?
Yes. The testmodel package gives you a deterministic fake model, and the examples run offline.

Does it support MCP?
Yes. The mcp package is a client for stdio and streamable HTTP servers, and mcpserver exposes an agent as an MCP tool.

When retrying isn't enough, model.NewFallback(primary, backup) tries models in order. For streams there's one rule: a fallback only happens before the first fragment is forwarded, because after the caller has seen output, switching models would replay it.

How do you stop a runaway agent?

Two limits cover it. golem.UsageLimit bounds input, output and total tokens, model requests and tool calls, and a dollar cost if you supply a price table with WithPrice. Token counts come from the provider's reported usage, so a token limit only trips when the provider reports usage, while requests and tool calls are counted by the run itself. Pricing is yours to supply, because I don't want to ship a table that goes stale between releases, and the library says plainly that the cost estimate is only as good as your rates and isn't a billing guarantee.

The second limit is loop detection, added in v1.2.0 (ADR 0051). WithLoopDetection(maxRepeats) counts calls to the same tool with canonically equal arguments across the whole run, and fails the run before the offending call executes. That ordering is the point: a model that polls a tool can't repeat a side effect while you wait for the check. WithLoopPolicy adds checks for repeated results, alternating A-B calls and repeated final text, with a choice between stopping the run and nudging the model.

Oversized tool output is the quieter cost. WithToolOutputLimit caps a tool result before it enters the conversation, keeps the head and tail, and appends a marker with the original size (ADR 0050).

What do you keep when a run fails?

When a run fails on turn six, you still want turns one to five. Golem attaches them to the error as RunError.Partial: the conversation through the last completed turn, the usage so far and the counts of requests and tool executions. Pass Partial.Messages to RunWithHistory to resume instead of starting over, which matters when the run has already spent real money.

How does an agent wait for a person?

Some tools shouldn't run without sign-off: deleting files, moving money, sending email. A tool defers by returning an error wrapping *tool.Deferred, of kind tool.DeferApproval or tool.DeferExternal. The other tool calls in that batch execute, and Run returns successfully with Result.Pending listing what's waiting. No further model call happens.

You resume with RunWithDeferredResults, passing the paused conversation and a decision for each pending call. Approved calls run, denied calls tell the model it was denied, and external results are inserted as given. Because a pause is a returned value, you can store it, show it in a UI and resume it hours later from another process. The reasoning behind that boundary is in the case for keeping meaningful actions with people.

Can a Go agent use MCP?

The Model Context Protocol is now the usual way to expose tools to agents, so Golem includes a client. mcp.NewStdio starts a server as a subprocess, mcp.NewHTTP connects to a remote endpoint, and mcp.AsTools turns the server's tool list into ordinary tool.Tool values with the server's own schema. A server error flagged as isError comes back as a correctable ModelRetry, and protocol or transport failures fail the run instead of being quietly corrected.

The guide says one thing I agree with: don't reach for MCP when a typed Go tool is one function away. A subprocess speaking JSON-RPC has more moving parts than a function call.

How do you test an agent without a model?

Agent tests are usually flaky (a real provider) or meaningless (mocked HTTP). Golem ships testmodel, a scripted in-memory model that plays back the responses you queue and records the exact request the agent sent:

client := testmodel.New().Respond(
    model.Response{Message: model.Message{Role: model.RoleAssistant, Content: "pong"}},
)
agent, _ := golem.New[struct{}, string](client, decoder)
result, err := agent.Run(context.Background(), golem.RunContext[struct{}]{}, "ping")

You can assert on the normalized request, the ordered messages in Result.Messages and which stage failed, with no network, keys or sleeps. The repository's CI runs its suite with the race detector, plus a fuzz target on the message JSON format.

How does it compare with other Go agent frameworks?

I compared Golem with the three other Go options I'd look at: langchaingo, Eino and Genkit for Go. I read each repository's source tree and go.mod on 27 November 2026. Dependency counts are the non-indirect lines in the require block, so they're approximate, and frameworks move fast, so check upstream before you depend on a detail.

Golem langchaingo Eino Genkit (Go)
Direct dependencies 0 About 60 About 10 About 40
License MIT MIT Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0
MCP client In the core module Not in the repository Separate eino-ext module Plugin in the repository, client and server
Pause for human approval tool.Deferred, resumable Not found Interrupt and resume in adk Tool approval middleware
Retry and model fallback Built into the run Not found Retry and failover in adk Retry and fallback middleware
Design centre One explicit agent loop with typed dependencies LangChain-style chains and agents Graph and workflow composition Flows with OpenTelemetry tracing

Two things stand out. Golem is the only one with no dependencies outside the standard library, and the only one where a tool receives a typed dependency value for the run. I haven't found an equivalent of RunContext[Deps] in the others, but I haven't audited every API, so read that as what I found, not a proof.

The other half is that Golem is not alone on the guardrails. Genkit's Go module ships MCP, retry, fallback and tool approval as plugins and middleware, and Eino's adk package has retry, failover and interrupt-and-resume. Only langchaingo lacks them in the repositories I read. The Golem README understated Genkit on this.

The others are ahead in other places. Eino's graph model is more expressive than Golem's linear loop for branching, parallel and multi-agent pipelines, and it has more community components. langchaingo covers more providers and vector stores. Genkit has first-party Google tooling and tight Gemini integration. What Golem offers is a smaller surface: one runtime for a single agent inside a service, with the controls in the core module instead of in add-on packages.

When should you pick something else?

Pick Golem if you want agents inside a Go service, typed dependencies, a module with nothing else to audit and tests that run offline. Pick something else if your agent is mostly prompt experimentation, if you need a graph engine for complicated multi-agent pipelines, or if you need a large catalog of prebuilt integrations today. Python is still ahead on that last one, and I won't pretend otherwise. Golem also has no evaluation harness and no durable workflow engine, and v1.0.0 lists both as non-goals.

Herbie, a self-hosted chat and workflow app I built, runs its Go backend on Golem. I don't have production numbers to publish yet, so everything above is design reasoning plus what the repository's tests and examples show.

The documentation site has a guide for each feature, and examples/ has runnable programs for nearly all of them, several with no API key.

  • Project page: the Golem overview and capability matrix
  • Repository: github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem
  • Docs: abubakarsiddik31.github.io/golem
  • API reference: pkg.go.dev/github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem

Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you try it and something feels un-Go-like, I want to hear about it.

Frequently asked questions

What is Golem?
Golem is an open-source AI agent framework for Go. It provides typed agents, tools with dependency injection, structured output, MCP support, and controls like retries, usage limits, loop detection and human approval.

Does Golem have external dependencies?
No. It uses only the Go standard library.

Which LLM providers does it support?
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and local models through Ollama, LM Studio or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Can I test agents without calling an API?
Yes. The testmodel package gives you a deterministic fake model, and the examples run offline.

Does it support MCP?
Yes. The mcp package is a client for stdio and streamable HTTP servers, and mcpserver exposes an agent as an MCP tool.

title: Your Grant Auditor Can Ask About Your AI Agent Years From Now. Can You Answer?
summary:
A how-to for compliance-heavy European organisations that run on public money: universities, research institutes, public hospitals, municipalities, agencies, NGOs and companies in EU-funded consortia.

If your organisation depends on government or EU funding, you already live with a particular kind of accountability. Every euro has conditions. Every claim needs evidence. Auditors can arrive long after the work is done, and what they find can be extended to other grants and recovered with money you may have already spent.

Now add AI agents. They draft cost statements, classify expenses, answer citizens, triage applications, prepare reports and pull data from systems of record. Each of those tasks touches an obligation. And a year or three later, an auditor, a funder, a regulator or a citizen asks the same simple question: how was this decided, and can you show us?

This guide explains why publicly funded organisations face that question earlier and harder than most, how to map agent work to the obligations it touches, and how to build the record that lets you answer. It closes with a 30 day plan.

A note on scope. This is general information, not legal or audit advice. Funding rules differ by programme and member state, so check your grant agreement, national rules and your own legal and audit advisers. The case is an illustrative composite with invented names. Parameter names in code are illustrative. ZizkaDB records events and shows whether the record has been altered. It does not decide eligibility, make a system compliant or replace your audit function.

Why funded organisations are different

Four features set publicly funded bodies apart.

  1. Your costs are conditional. Funding is paid against rules on what counts as an eligible cost. If a cost is later found ineligible, it can be recovered. Under the Horizon Europe model grant agreement, beneficiaries must keep records and supporting documents to confirm proper use of funds and the costs claimed, and a published guide summarising the rules says records must be kept for five years after the final payment for grants over 60,000 euros, or three years for grants of 60,000 euros or less. A national contact point for Horizon Europe adds that the period can be longer in case of ongoing audits or national requirements. Other EU programmes and national funders have their own conditions, so check yours.

  2. Many bodies can audit you, and findings can travel. The model grant agreement includes provisions for checks, reviews and audits, including by OLAF, the European Public Prosecutor's Office and the European Court of Auditors, and a clause on the consequences of audits that deals with extension of findings. In plain terms, a weakness found in one project can prompt questions about others that used the same process. An agent that applied the same classification rule across thirty grants is one finding multiplied by thirty.

  3. Public-law rules on AI apply to you directly. The EU AI Act asks deployers of certain high-risk AI systems that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, to perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before use, and to notify the market surveillance authority of the results. Deployers of high-risk systems must also keep the logs the system generates, where under their control, for at least six months. The Digital Omnibus moved the application date for Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027, so check the final text and your timeline. Which of your systems count as high-risk depends on what they do, and that includes systems used to assess eligibility for public benefits and services.

  4. Cyber and incident rules are stricter for public bodies. Under NIS2, public administration entities of central governments are essential entities, regional ones are covered on a risk basis, and member states may extend coverage to local governments. A significant incident triggers an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month. If an agent is involved in an incident, you need to reconstruct what it did quickly.

Add to this the usual public-sector layer: data protection law, public procurement rules, freedom of information duties in many countries, and the expectation that public money is spent transparently. The result is an organisation that is asked to prove its decisions more often than almost any other.

The case: the research office and the cost classification agent

This is a composite, with invented names. A university research office, call it Northfield University, uses an AI agent to prepare the cost statements for dozens of EU and national grants. The agent reads time records, invoices and payroll extracts, classifies each item against the cost categories in each grant agreement, and drafts the periodic financial report. A research accountant reviews a sample before submission.

Year one. The agent classifies a recurring item, a shared equipment service contract, as a direct eligible cost for twelve projects. A prompt update in month five changes how it reads certain invoice descriptions. Staff turnover follows. The accountant who set up the review sample leaves.

Year three. After final payment, a funder audit selects one of the projects. The auditor asks about the service contract cost: why was it classified as direct eligible, which version of the grant rules was applied, what evidence supported it, who verified it, and was the same treatment applied elsewhere?

What Northfield has. The final report, the invoices and some application logs. The logs show the output, not the reasoning inputs. The prompt version in force that month is unclear. The reviewer has left. The agent's classification of the same item in other projects cannot be listed without re-running the whole year.

What the auditor does. Finds the cost ineligible in this project, and asks whether the treatment applies to other grants. The university spends weeks reconstructing, and the answers are partly guesses. Recovery is demanded on the one project, and the finding is extended to the others.

None of this requires fraud. It requires only that nobody could show how the decision was made.

What an auditor, funder or regulator will ask
What source documents did the agent use for this item?
Which version of the grant rules and which cost category definitions applied?
Why was it classified this way?
Who verified it, what did they see and when?
Which model, prompt and configuration were in force?
How many other items and projects were treated the same way?
Has the record been altered since?
Can you produce it for the full retention period?
Why ordinary logs fail the funded organisation
They rotate long before the retention period ends, which can be five years or more after final payment.
They record outputs, not the sources, rules and versions behind them.
They cannot list everything affected by one faulty rule.
They do not show who reviewed what.
They can be edited, and an auditor's first question about any record is whether it is original.
They sit in vendor systems you may no longer have access to when the audit arrives.
Step 1: map agent work to obligations

Start with a register, not with technology. List every task an agent performs, and for each one record which obligation it touches.

Agent task Obligation touched Evidence needed later
Classify costs against grant categories Eligibility of costs, record keeping, audit Source docs, rule version, classification, reviewer
Draft periodic technical or financial reports Reporting accuracy Inputs, draft, edits, approver
Answer citizen or applicant questions Duty of care, transparency Question, sources used, answer, handoff
Triage applications or benefits Fundamental rights, non-discrimination, explanation Inputs, criteria, outcome, human review
Draft procurement documents Procurement rules Sources, changes, approver
Handle incidents or alerts NIS2 reporting, security Timeline, actions, evidence

For every row, name an owner. A task without an owner will not have evidence.

Step 2: record decisions as linked chains tied to the funding context

Each decision should be linked to the grant, work package or programme it affects, so that an audit by grant, by rule or by period is a query and not a project.

python
src = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="source_item",
data={"grant": "HE-101012345", "wp": "WP3", "item_ref": "INV-77421",
"doc_sha256": "", "period": "RP2"})

rule = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="rules_applied",
data={"grant_rules": "HE-MGA v1.2 Art 6", "national_rules": "UNI-POLICY-2026-04",
"category_table_v": "9", "prompt_v": "v18", "model": "provider-model-2026-03"},
parent_id=src.id)

cls = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="classification",
data={"category": "direct_equipment_service", "eligible": True,
"basis": ["service contract used only for project equipment"],
"confidence": "medium"},
parent_id=rule.id)

Store references and digests of documents, not full copies, and apply redaction before storage for personal data.

Step 3: separate agent judgment from verified decisions

Where money or rights depend on a decision, record the human step with what the person saw.

python
rev = await db.log(agent="research-accounts", event="human_review",
data={"reviewer": "u-acct-12", "saw": ["invoice", "contract", "classification_basis"],
"action": "confirmed", "sample_type": "risk_based"},
parent_id=cls.id)

Do not log only that someone clicked approve. Log what they were shown, what they changed and why. An auditor will weigh a review more heavily when it shows engagement with evidence.

Step 4: add rules outside the model for the costly mistakes

Put deterministic checks around the decisions that matter most. Examples for a research office: a cost above a threshold needs human review, a cost type flagged as ineligible by the programme's rules cannot be marked eligible by the agent, and an item that matches a known risky pattern, such as shared equipment or overheads, must be flagged.

python
await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="rule_check",
data={"rule": "shared_equipment_needs_review", "result": "flag", "blocking": True},
parent_id=cls.id)

A flagged item is held for review. The audit record explains afterwards. The rule prevents.

Step 5: use impact queries to answer extension of findings

When an auditor, or your own review, finds a faulty rule, prompt version or classification pattern, you need to know every item that used it, across every grant.

python
affected = await db.impact(rule.id)

Use it before the funder asks. List the items, correct or document each, and approach the funder with a complete picture. Voluntarily scoping and correcting a problem is a stronger position than having it extended to you.

Step 6: align retention with the funding clock

Set retention from the longest obligation that applies, not from your IT default.

Funding. At least the period in the grant agreement, such as five years after final payment for larger Horizon Europe grants, and longer if an audit is open or national rules require.
Legal hold. When an audit, investigation or dispute starts, suspend deletion for the relevant records.
Data protection. Keep personal data only as long as needed, and decide in advance how erasure requests interact with an integrity-protected record. ZizkaDB supports redaction before storage and forget with tombstones, and your data protection officer should approve the approach.
Exportability. Export and archive before systems are retired, and test that archives can be re-imported and verified.
python
export = await db.export_events(agent="grants-cost-agent", since="2026-01-01", until="2026-06-30")
Step 7: make the record tamper evident, with custody you can defend

Every event in ZizkaDB carries a SHA-256 checksum chained to the previous one for that agent. Any edit, deletion or reordering breaks the chain. Verify on a schedule and store the chain head somewhere your own system administrators cannot edit, such as your records management system or your internal audit function.

python
check = await db.verify_chain(agent="grants-cost-agent")

store check.head with internal audit, and log the verification date

When an auditor asks whether the record is original, you can show a verification result and the independently held head. That proves the record has not changed since the head was stored. It does not prove the record was complete.

Step 8: prepare for the incident clock

If an agent is involved in a security or data incident, NIS2-type reporting starts at awareness: early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours, final report within one month. Prepare in advance. Make sure you can freeze and export the relevant chain, list every action the agent took in the window, scope affected records through the impact query, and show who did what during the response. Our incident response how-to covers the 72 hour runbook in more detail.

Step 9: give auditors a clean, safe way in

Create an audit access procedure before you need it.

Use read-only, expiring keys scoped to the grant, period or decision set requested.
Provide a standard export with the chain verification result.
Keep a log of who accessed what.
Run a dry audit once a year with someone outside the team.
python
await db.log(agent="audit-desk", event="auditor_access_granted",
data={"auditor_org": "funder-audit-unit", "scope": "grant HE-101012345",
"expires": "2026-12-31", "approved_by": "u-compliance-3"})
Step 10: choose infrastructure that fits public-sector constraints

Publicly funded bodies often face procurement rules, data residency expectations, sovereignty concerns and vendor exit requirements. Design for them.

Self host inside your own environment or an EU-based environment you control, so the evidence stays in your custody.
Avoid lock-in. Choose tools that are open source, so your team and your auditors can inspect the code, and that are model, LLM and cloud agnostic, so you can change providers without losing history.
Keep it small. A single container on Postgres is easier to secure, accredit and operate than a sprawling platform.
Plan exit. Test exporting and re-importing your records.

ZizkaDB's core is AGPL-3.0, runs self hosted in a single Docker container, and can be placed inside the environment you choose. Whether it meets your security and procurement requirements is for your own teams to decide.

Business objectives and how to measure them
Objective Measure
Protect funding from recovery Share of audited items with a complete evidence chain; ineligible cost found per audit
Cut audit preparation time Hours to answer an auditor request, before and after
Contain a finding early Time from discovering a faulty rule to listing all affected items
Support AI governance duties Share of agent decisions with a full record; FRIA evidence ready
Strengthen future bids and procurement positions Evidence packs provided to funders and partners on request
Reduce reputational risk Citizen complaints resolved with a verifiable account
An illustrative exposure example

This is invented, to show the logic. A university manages 40 EU and national grants worth 20 million euros over the reporting period. If a systematic classification weakness caused 2 percent of the claimed costs to be later found ineligible, the exposure would be 400,000 euros, before the cost of the audit itself and the staff time to rebuild evidence. Even a modest reduction in that risk, or in the time to scope it, can justify the effort of recording decisions properly. Use your own figures.

Common mistakes
Treating AI as an IT matter. The obligations belong to finance, research administration, legal and service owners, not only to the technology team.
Keeping logs for 30 days and grants for 5 years. The shortest retention in the chain sets your real position.
Letting an agent decide eligibility alone. Put rules and human review around money and rights.
Recording output only. An auditor needs sources, rules and versions.
Forgetting the review step. Show what the reviewer saw.
One copy, one custodian. Store the chain head elsewhere.
Assuming the vendor holds the evidence. If the contract ends, so can your access.
Ignoring erasure. Decide the approach before the first request.
A 30 day plan

Days 1 to 5: build the obligation register. List agent tasks, the obligation each touches, the retention period that applies and an owner.
Days 6 to 10: choose one high-value workflow, such as cost classification, and define its event model with research administration, legal and your data protection officer.
Days 11 to 15: instrument the workflow with source, rules, classification and review events, and add the blocking rules for the highest risk items.
Days 16 to 20: set retention and legal hold, test export and re-import, and verify the hash chain with the head held by internal audit.
Days 21 to 25: run an impact query on a seeded faulty rule and measure how fast you can list affected items across grants.
Days 26 to 30: run a mock audit with someone outside the team using the eight questions above. Record the gaps, assign owners and agree the next workflow.

Where ZizkaDB fits, and its limits

ZizkaDB is an open source causal audit database for AI agents. It records each decision as a linked event, answers why() for any outcome, lists everything downstream of a faulty input through the impact route, supports replay and drift baselines, and shows whether stored history has been altered through a SHA-256 hash chain. It is model, LLM and cloud agnostic, and it runs self hosted in a single Docker container, with a managed Cloud edition at db.zizka.ai for multi-agent setups.

It does not decide whether a cost is eligible, assess fundamental rights impacts, report incidents or make a body compliant with any rule. It records what your system captures, so the rules and reviews you add are what prevent errors. The open source edition records one agent per install, so fleets and agent to agent flows use the Cloud edition or separate instances. Take advice from your legal, audit and data protection teams on retention, erasure and what the funder requires.

If you rely on public money and use AI agents, choose one funded workflow this week and trace one claimed cost from the source document to the final report. If you can do it in minutes and show the record is original, you are ready for the audit. If you cannot, you have found the gap before the auditor did.

Start with a register, not with technology. List every task an agent performs, and for each one record which obligation it touches.

Agent task Obligation touched Evidence needed later
Classify costs against grant categories Eligibility of costs, record keeping, audit Source docs, rule version, classification, reviewer
Draft periodic technical or financial reports Reporting accuracy Inputs, draft, edits, approver
Answer citizen or applicant questions Duty of care, transparency Question, sources used, answer, handoff
Triage applications or benefits Fundamental rights, non-discrimination, explanation Inputs, criteria, outcome, human review
Draft procurement documents Procurement rules Sources, changes, approver
Handle incidents or alerts NIS2 reporting, security Timeline, actions, evidence

For every row, name an owner. A task without an owner will not have evidence.

Step 2: record decisions as linked chains tied to the funding context

Each decision should be linked to the grant, work package or programme it affects, so that an audit by grant, by rule or by period is a query and not a project.

python
src = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="source_item",
data={"grant": "HE-101012345", "wp": "WP3", "item_ref": "INV-77421",
"doc_sha256": "", "period": "RP2"})

rule = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="rules_applied",
data={"grant_rules": "HE-MGA v1.2 Art 6", "national_rules": "UNI-POLICY-2026-04",
"category_table_v": "9", "prompt_v": "v18", "model": "provider-model-2026-03"},
parent_id=src.id)

cls = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="classification",
data={"category": "direct_equipment_service", "eligible": True,
"basis": ["service contract used only for project equipment"],
"confidence": "medium"},
parent_id=rule.id)

Store references and digests of documents, not full copies, and apply redaction before storage for personal data.

Step 3: separate agent judgment from verified decisions

Where money or rights depend on a decision, record the human step with what the person saw.

python
rev = await db.log(agent="research-accounts", event="human_review",
data={"reviewer": "u-acct-12", "saw": ["invoice", "contract", "classification_basis"],
"action": "confirmed", "sample_type": "risk_based"},
parent_id=cls.id)

Do not log only that someone clicked approve. Log what they were shown, what they changed and why. An auditor will weigh a review more heavily when it shows engagement with evidence.

Step 4: add rules outside the model for the costly mistakes

Put deterministic checks around the decisions that matter most. Examples for a research office: a cost above a threshold needs human review, a cost type flagged as ineligible by the programme's rules cannot be marked eligible by the agent, and an item that matches a known risky pattern, such as shared equipment or overheads, must be flagged.

python
await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="rule_check",
data={"rule": "shared_equipment_needs_review", "result": "flag", "blocking": True},
parent_id=cls.id)

A flagged item is held for review. The audit record explains afterwards. The rule prevents.

Step 5: use impact queries to answer extension of findings

When an auditor, or your own review, finds a faulty rule, prompt version or classification pattern, you need to know every item that used it, across every grant.

python
affected = await db.impact(rule.id)

Use it before the funder asks. List the items, correct or document each, and approach the funder with a complete picture. Voluntarily scoping and correcting a problem is a stronger position than having it extended to you.

Step 6: align retention with the funding clock

Set retention from the longest obligation that applies, not from your IT default.

Funding. At least the period in the grant agreement, such as five years after final payment for larger Horizon Europe grants, and longer if an audit is open or national rules require.
Legal hold. When an audit, investigation or dispute starts, suspend deletion for the relevant records.
Data protection. Keep personal data only as long as needed, and decide in advance how erasure requests interact with an integrity-protected record. ZizkaDB supports redaction before storage and forget with tombstones, and your data protection officer should approve the approach.
Exportability. Export and archive before systems are retired, and test that archives can be re-imported and verified.
python
export = await db.export_events(agent="grants-cost-agent", since="2026-01-01", until="2026-06-30")
Step 7: make the record tamper evident, with custody you can defend

Every event in ZizkaDB carries a SHA-256 checksum chained to the previous one for that agent. Any edit, deletion or reordering breaks the chain. Verify on a schedule and store the chain head somewhere your own system administrators cannot edit, such as your records management system or your internal audit function.

python
check = await db.verify_chain(agent="grants-cost-agent")

store check.head with internal audit, and log the verification date

When an auditor asks whether the record is original, you can show a verification result and the independently held head. That proves the record has not changed since the head was stored. It does not prove the record was complete.

Step 8: prepare for the incident clock

If an agent is involved in a security or data incident, NIS2-type reporting starts at awareness: early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours, final report within one month. Prepare in advance. Make sure you can freeze and export the relevant chain, list every action the agent took in the window, scope affected records through the impact query, and show who did what during the response. Our incident response how-to covers the 72 hour runbook in more detail.

Step 9: give auditors a clean, safe way in

Create an audit access procedure before you need it.

Use read-only, expiring keys scoped to the grant, period or decision set requested.
Provide a standard export with the chain verification result.
Keep a log of who accessed what.
Run a dry audit once a year with someone outside the team.
python
await db.log(agent="audit-desk", event="auditor_access_granted",
data={"auditor_org": "funder-audit-unit", "scope": "grant HE-101012345",
"expires": "2026-12-31", "approved_by": "u-compliance-3"})
Step 10: choose infrastructure that fits public-sector constraints

Publicly funded bodies often face procurement rules, data residency expectations, sovereignty concerns and vendor exit requirements. Design for them.

Self host inside your own environment or an EU-based environment you control, so the evidence stays in your custody.
Avoid lock-in. Choose tools that are open source, so your team and your auditors can inspect the code, and that are model, LLM and cloud agnostic, so you can change providers without losing history.
Keep it small. A single container on Postgres is easier to secure, accredit and operate than a sprawling platform.
Plan exit. Test exporting and re-importing your records.

ZizkaDB's core is AGPL-3.0, runs self hosted in a single Docker container, and can be placed inside the environment you choose. Whether it meets your security and procurement requirements is for your own teams to decide.

Business objectives and how to measure them
Objective Measure
Protect funding from recovery Share of audited items with a complete evidence chain; ineligible cost found per audit
Cut audit preparation time Hours to answer an auditor request, before and after
Contain a finding early Time from discovering a faulty rule to listing all affected items
Support AI governance duties Share of agent decisions with a full record; FRIA evidence ready
Strengthen future bids and procurement positions Evidence packs provided to funders and partners on request
Reduce reputational risk Citizen complaints resolved with a verifiable account
An illustrative exposure example

This is invented, to show the logic. A university manages 40 EU and national grants worth 20 million euros over the reporting period. If a systematic classification weakness caused 2 percent of the claimed costs to be later found ineligible, the exposure would be 400,000 euros, before the cost of the audit itself and the staff time to rebuild evidence. Even a modest reduction in that risk, or in the time to scope it, can justify the effort of recording decisions properly. Use your own figures.

Common mistakes
Treating AI as an IT matter. The obligations belong to finance, research administration, legal and service owners, not only to the technology team.
Keeping logs for 30 days and grants for 5 years. The shortest retention in the chain sets your real position.
Letting an agent decide eligibility alone. Put rules and human review around money and rights.
Recording output only. An auditor needs sources, rules and versions.
Forgetting the review step. Show what the reviewer saw.
One copy, one custodian. Store the chain head elsewhere.
Assuming the vendor holds the evidence. If the contract ends, so can your access.
Ignoring erasure. Decide the approach before the first request.
A 30 day plan

Days 1 to 5: build the obligation register. List agent tasks, the obligation each touches, the retention period that applies and an owner.
Days 6 to 10: choose one high-value workflow, such as cost classification, and define its event model with research administration, legal and your data protection officer.
Days 11 to 15: instrument the workflow with source, rules, classification and review events, and add the blocking rules for the highest risk items.
Days 16 to 20: set retention and legal hold, test export and re-import, and verify the hash chain with the head held by internal audit.
Days 21 to 25: run an impact query on a seeded faulty rule and measure how fast you can list affected items across grants.
Days 26 to 30: run a mock audit with someone outside the team using the eight questions above. Record the gaps, assign owners and agree the next workflow.

Where ZizkaDB fits, and its limits

ZizkaDB is an open source causal audit database for AI agents. It records each decision as a linked event, answers why() for any outcome, lists everything downstream of a faulty input through the impact route, supports replay and drift baselines, and shows whether stored history has been altered through a SHA-256 hash chain. It is model, LLM and cloud agnostic, and it runs self hosted in a single Docker container, with a managed Cloud edition at db.zizka.ai for multi-agent setups.

It does not decide whether a cost is eligible, assess fundamental rights impacts, report incidents or make a body compliant with any rule. It records what your system captures, so the rules and reviews you add are what prevent errors. The open source edition records one agent per install, so fleets and agent to agent flows use the Cloud edition or separate instances. Take advice from your legal, audit and data protection teams on retention, erasure and what the funder requires.

If you rely on public money and use AI agents, choose one funded workflow this week and trace one claimed cost from the source document to the final report. If you can do it in minutes and show the record is original, you are ready for the audit. If you cannot, you have found the gap before the auditor did.

title: Writing numbers in Vietnamese words: the rules that break every number-to-words library
summary:
If you've ever generated invoices for Vietnam, you've hit this requirement: the total must be written in numbers and in words. 1.250.000 ₫ has to become Một triệu hai trăm năm mươi nghìn đồng.

Generic number-to-words libraries get Vietnamese wrong in at least five places. Here they are, with the code that handles them.

1. A zero tens digit is read "linh" (or "lẻ")

105 is not "một trăm năm" – that would mean 150 in casual speech. It's một trăm linh năm. Southern speakers say lẻ, so make it an option.

2. "mười" vs "mươi"

10–19 use mười (ten). 20–99 use mươi after the tens digit: 30 = ba mươi. Same letters, different tone mark – and a different word.

3. The units digit changes its name

  • 1 after 20+ becomes mốt: 21 = hai mươi mốt (but 11 = mười một)
  • 5 after any tens becomes lăm: 15 = mười lăm, 25 = hai mươi lăm (but 105 = một trăm linh năm)
  • 4 after 20+ is usually tư: 24 = hai mươi tư (but 14 = mười bốn)

4. "không trăm" in the middle

1.005.000 is read một triệu không trăm linh năm nghìn. Accountants want the explicit không trăm (zero hundred) so nobody can alter the amount. Groups that are entirely zero are skipped, so 1.000.005 is just một triệu không trăm linh năm – no "không nghìn".

5. Billions nest

There's no word for 10^12. 1.500 billion is một nghìn năm trăm tỷ – "one thousand five hundred billion".

The core: reading one 3-digit group

Everything above lives in one small function. full means "this group is not the first one", so it must read không trăm and linh explicitly:

const D = ['không','một','hai','ba','bốn','năm','sáu','bảy','tám','chín'];

function readTriple(n, full) {               // n: 0..999
  const h = Math.floor(n / 100), t = Math.floor(n / 10) % 10, u = n % 10, w = [];
  if (h || full) w.push(D[h], 'trăm');
  if (t === 0 && u && (h || full)) w.push('linh');       // 105 → một trăm linh năm
  else if (t === 1) w.push('mười');
  else if (t > 1) w.push(D[t], 'mươi');
  if (u === 1 && t > 1) w.push('mốt');                   // 21 → hai mươi mốt
  else if (u === 4 && t > 1) w.push('tư');               // 24 → hai mươi tư
  else if (u === 5 && t > 0) w.push('lăm');              // 15, 25 → mười lăm, hai mươi lăm
  else if (u) w.push(D[u]);
  return w;
}

Split the number into groups of three from the right, read each non-zero group, append nghìn / triệu / tỷ, and you're 90% there. Use BigInt or plain digit strings – invoice totals in VND overflow Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER faster than you'd think once you hit 16 digits.

The other 10%: parsing what people type

Vietnamese users type 1.250.000, 1,250,000, 1,25 triệu, 1tr250, 500k, 1 tỷ 250 triệu. A dot or comma before exactly three digits is a thousands separator; otherwise it's a decimal. That one rule resolves almost every ambiguity.

Open source + a free tool

I packaged all of this as doc-so-tien (MIT, zero dependencies), including an English "amount in words" reader for VND/USD/EUR, an Excel VBA function =DocSoTien(A1) and a Google Sheets =DOCSOTIEN(A1). The JS, VBA and Apps Script versions are cross-checked on 40,000+ numbers.

If you just need the words, it runs at docso.co – paste one number or a whole Excel column, everything computed in your browser.

Found a reading I got wrong? Tell me in the comments.

title: DeepSeek Harness Setup & Troubleshooting: Node 24.9, PTC Mode, Custom API, and Plugins
summary:
When I first tried running npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web on my Windows machine to test DeepSeek Harness (dsh 0.2.2-rc.5), my terminal immediately threw an engine mismatch error because my system Node was sitting at v22.22.2. Even after I got the app open, the plugin list looked nearly bare, my first file-writing task failed inside the PowerShell sandbox, and I wasn't sure how to wire in my own OpenAI-compatible API key without breaking ~/.dsh/cordis.patch.yml.

I spent the afternoon working through each of those roadblocks on Windows: getting around the node >=24.9.0 requirement, testing how PTC mode prevents context window blowouts on batch jobs, connecting a unified custom API provider to crunch a 9-row Q3 sales CSV, installing 8 community plugins, and using Creator mode to build a 3,000-line knowledge graph extension from scratch.

If you just installed dsh, here is the biggest takeaway from my run: switching to the right execution mode matters much more than loading up on plugins. Running a 300-file audit in Standard mode will flood your context window with intermediate tool outputs, whereas PTC mode writes a script to process the batch locally and returns only the final summary. And if you only use dsh for quick single-turn coding questions with a single model, stick to the default login—you don't need custom provider patches at all.

Common Scenario or Error What to Do in dsh Why It Happens / What to Watch Out For
CLI fails to start on node < 24.9.0 Install the Desktop App (or upgrade Node LTS and restart terminal) The npm package requires node >=24.9.0, while the Desktop installer bundles its own isolated runtime
PowerShell sandbox write error when saving files Switch bottom-left permissions from Read-Only to Workspace Write Read-Only blocks disk writes; Workspace Write allows file creation inside your project folder without exposing your whole OS
404 POST /v1/chat/completions/chat/completions Set Custom API URL strictly up to /v1 dsh automatically appends /chat/completions to the base URL
PI_AI_ERROR: No API key for provider on startup Keep the apiKeyEnv field inside ~/.dsh/cordis.patch.yml Omitting apiKeyEnv when editing the YAML patch file causes the process to exit immediately
Context window overflows during multi-file checks Switch top-left selector to PTC Mode (PTC模式) Model writes and executes a local program in one pass so intermediate data stays out of chat history
Want to add a new UI button or sidebar view Switch to Creator Mode (创造模式) Includes the plugin-authoring skill; generated and auto-mounted 7 files (3,000+ lines) in ~21 minutes

Environment Pitfalls, Permission Boundaries, and Workspace Privacy

Before installing plugins or changing model configs, it helps to clear the four environment traps I ran into on my first launch.

Main workspace layout: collapsible navigation sidebar on the left, chat composer in the center, and mode, permission, and model controls along the bottom bar.

1. The Node.js 24.9 Threshold: CLI vs. Desktop Installer

DeepSeek Harness offers two installation paths, and they handle Node versions very differently:

  • npm CLI (npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web): Requires node >=24.9.0. By default, it starts a local server on http://127.0.0.1:3080 and opens your browser (pass --no-open if you are running it on a headless server or over SSH). If you upgrade Node on Windows after seeing a version error, you must close and reopen your terminal window so the updated PATH refreshes.
  • Desktop Installer: Bundles its own Node runtime. Because my Windows system was running v22.22.2 and I didn't want to touch my global environment for other projects, I installed the Desktop app and went straight into the main UI.

Also note that dsh displays a Developer Preview notice on first launch. Because plugin IDs and YAML keys can change between preview builds, always check dsh --version first (everything below was tested on 0.2.2-rc.5).

2. Why My First File Write Failed: The Three Permission Tiers

At the bottom left of the input box sits the permission selector:

The permission menu at the bottom left: Read-Only, Workspace Write, and Full Access.

  • Read-Only (仅可查看): The agent can read files inside the workspace but cannot modify or create anything. When I first asked dsh to generate a markdown report from a CSV file, I forgot the toggle was sitting on Read-Only, and the task immediately threw a PowerShell sandbox write error.
  • Workspace Write (工作区内修改): Allows reading, creating, and editing files strictly inside the active workspace directory. This is the safest default for daily work.
  • Full Access (完全权限): Grants unrestricted read/write access across your entire computer. While it stops confirmation prompts, a single mistyped prompt can alter system directories outside your project. If you ever turn on Full Access, create a dedicated empty folder on your drive first and use that as your workspace boundary.

3. The Workspace Dropdown Privacy Trap

Every conversation in dsh requires selecting a Workspace above the input box, which maps directly to a real directory on your hard drive. When you click the workspace dropdown menu to switch projects, dsh displays the full names of every local folder you have opened in the past. Always collapse the left sidebar before taking screenshots or recording your screen so you don't accidentally publish your local directory structure.

PTC Mode vs. Standard Mode: Why Execution Modes Are Plugins Too

Why do people call DeepSeek Harness an "everything is a plugin" alternative to Claude Code?

In tools like Claude Code, model invocation, built-in tools, and session management are hardcoded into the base layer. DeepSeek Harness is built on top of the Cordis plugin framework. That means the model adapter (llm-pi-ai), context engine, session manager, tool runner, the UI panels, and all four execution modes are mounted as independent Cordis plugins. Because Cordis treats plugin registration as reversible side effects, you can swap modules in and out—and unloading a broken plugin cleanly rolls back every UI button and hook it registered.

Clicking the mode menu at the top left of the composer reveals four presets:

The four execution modes at the top left of the input box.

  1. Standard Mode (标准模式): Enables file read/write, shell commands, web search, skills, and sub-agents. This handles 80% of daily coding and editing.
  2. PTC Mode (PTC模式): The model writes a program to execute a multi-step workflow in a single pass. Intermediate outputs stay inside the execution environment instead of streaming back into the chat context.
  3. Creator Mode (创造模式): Standard mode plus the dedicated plugin-authoring skill for building new dsh extensions.
  4. Minimal Mode (极简模式): Strips the agent down to just the terminal and image reader for raw model benchmarking.

Here is where PTC Mode saves real money: suppose you need to audit 400 configuration files or count every error code across a massive log directory. In Standard mode, the agent reads files one by one in a loop, appending every intermediate file dump into the chat history until the context window overflows. In PTC mode, the agent writes a small script that scans all 400 files locally and only prints the final aggregated table into the conversation.

One practical tip from my testing: because PTC hides intermediate steps inside the script execution, debugging a wrong summary number is harder than in Standard mode. I always test my prompt on 2 or 3 sample files first to verify the calculation logic before unleashing PTC mode on a full directory.

Wiring in Crazyrouter Custom API and Running a 9-Row CSV Benchmark

When I started running multi-model comparisons and background summarization plugins in dsh, I wanted to put DeepSeek, Claude, and GPT under the same bottom-right model selector using a single API key.

Because dsh delegates model calls to the llm-pi-ai plugin (see the official DeepSeek Harness providers documentation for the underlying schema), you can wire in any OpenAI-compatible gateway directly from the settings UI. I connected Crazyrouter and ran a full tool-call verification.

1. Switching to the Custom Model API Tab and Configuring the 5 Fields

Navigate to Settings → Models (设置 → 模型) at the bottom left and click Add Model Provider (添加模型提供商) at the top right. Pay attention to the modal header: it opens on the built-in third-party provider list by default, so you must click the "Custom Model API" (自定义模型API) tab next to it to reveal the custom form.

Enter the Base URL in the API URL field:

https://api.crazyrouter.com/v1

Here is how I filled out the five fields and the two exact error messages I reproduced while testing bad inputs:

  • Provider ID: Use a lowercase string like crazyrouter. Once saved, session history and default model settings bind to this ID permanently; to rename it later, you have to create a new provider and delete the old one.
  • API Protocol: Select OpenAI Chat Completions.
  • API URL: Enter https://api.crazyrouter.com/v1 and do not append /chat/completions. When I tested pasting the full /v1/chat/completions path, dsh immediately threw a 404 error: POST /v1/chat/completions/chat/completions is not valid. Do not append /chat/completions twice.
  • API Key: Paste your key and save (the UI masks it afterward). If you prefer editing ~/.dsh/cordis.patch.yml directly in an editor, never delete the apiKeyEnv key—omitting it causes dsh to fail on startup with PI_AI_ERROR: No API key for provider.
  • Fetching the Model List (GET /models): I entered deepseek-v4.1-flash as an initial model ID and clicked Fetch Available Models (获取可用模型). dsh queried GET /models against the endpoint and pulled 185 available models in one click (including deepseek-v4-pro, glm-5.4, and claude-opus-4-8).

Before typing model IDs by hand, I always verify the exact identifier on the Crazyrouter model pricing catalog. Gateway model IDs (like deepseek-v4.1-flash) don't always match vendor marketing names character for character, and a typo triggers UNKNOWN_MODEL. If you also want to benchmark different AI coding models across dsh, Cursor, or Cline, that catalog lists the context limits and parameters side by side.

2. Verifying the Tool-Calling Loop on a Q3 Sales CSV

To verify that the custom endpoint handles multi-step tool execution—not just plain text chat—I dropped a 9-row sales.csv file (July–September 2026 revenue and order counts for East, North, and South regions) into my workspace. Using deepseek-v4.1-flash and deepseek-v4-pro through the custom provider, I asked dsh to calculate September month-over-month growth, rank Q3 regional revenue, compute average order value (AOV), and write the result to report.md.

With permissions set to Workspace Write, the agent read the CSV, ran the calculation, and wrote report.md in a single pass (15.1K tokens consumed, output speed 103 tok/s). I checked all 9 figures against the raw CSV by hand:

I spent the afternoon working through each of those roadblocks on Windows: getting around the node >=24.9.0 requirement, testing how PTC mode prevents context window blowouts on batch jobs, connecting a unified custom API provider to crunch a 9-row Q3 sales CSV, installing 8 community plugins, and using Creator mode to build a 3,000-line knowledge graph extension from scratch.

If you just installed dsh, here is the biggest takeaway from my run: switching to the right execution mode matters much more than loading up on plugins. Running a 300-file audit in Standard mode will flood your context window with intermediate tool outputs, whereas PTC mode writes a script to process the batch locally and returns only the final summary. And if you only use dsh for quick single-turn coding questions with a single model, stick to the default login—you don't need custom provider patches at all.

404 POST /v1/chat/completions/chat/completions Set Custom API URL strictly up to /v1 dsh automatically appends /chat/completions to the base URL

1. The Node.js 24.9 Threshold: CLI vs. Desktop Installer

If you upgrade Node on Windows after seeing a version error, you must close and reopen your terminal window so the updated PATH refreshes.
  • Desktop Installer: Bundles its own Node runtime. Because my Windows system was running v22.22.2 and I didn't want to touch my global environment for other projects, I installed the Desktop app and went straight into the main UI.

Also note that dsh displays a Developer Preview notice on first launch. Because plugin IDs and YAML keys can change between preview builds, always check dsh --version first (everything below was tested on 0.2.2-rc.5).

2. Why My First File Write Failed: The Three Permission Tiers

  • Read-Only (仅可查看): The agent can read files inside the workspace but cannot modify or create anything. When I first asked dsh to generate a markdown report from a CSV file, I forgot the toggle was sitting on Read-Only, and the task immediately threw a PowerShell sandbox write error.
  • Workspace Write (工作区内修改): Allows reading, creating, and editing files strictly inside the active workspace directory. This is the safest default for daily work.
  • Full Access (完全权限): Grants unrestricted read/write access across your entire computer. Why do people call DeepSeek Harness an "everything is a plugin" alternative to Claude Code?

In tools like Claude Code, model invocation, built-in tools, and session management are hardcoded into the base layer. DeepSeek Harness is built on top of the Cordis plugin framework. title: How my projects ended up at mAGI
summary:
Originally published at pankajgarkoti.github.io/blog-road-to-magi.

mAGI is a Fedora/Hyprland setup where the main interface is one LLM agent in tmux. Looking back at the repos, most of what I built over the last four years points at it. This post goes through them in order.

2022: a chatbot people talked to

At Hear Us I built Joy, a conversational bot for wellbeing check-ins. It ran on Slack, then on WhatsApp: a state machine on top of Dialogflow, with Firestore for events and conversation memory. This was before ChatGPT. It was the first thing I built that people talked to instead of clicking through.

The same year I started keeping my dotfiles on GitHub. Neovim and the terminal. Everything below lives there.

2023: one assistant, many specialists

At Mavex AI the product was Mavy, an executive assistant. The user talked to one thing; behind it a router sent each request to one of fourteen specialists: calendar, email, tasks, search and so on. Function calling was barely out, so the router was GPT-4 forced to return one of two JSON shapes: answer directly, or hand off. I wrote about it here. The search service behind it picked its retrieval cutoff by clustering similarity scores instead of using a fixed threshold (post).

One assistant in front, specialists behind it. mAGI has the same shape.

2024: agent loops and pipelines

I pulled the agent loop out into AgentZero, a minimal tool-calling agent. Its README has a wishlist. Two items:

  • long-running processes where working memory is summarised as execution goes on

  • a status check on a long task without interrupting it

Then PlanWeaver, a plan-and-execute agent, and ChainFactory: a small DSL for chaining LLM calls, with parallel steps and typed outputs, published on PyPI as chainfactory-py. The spec drafts are on this site.

2025: notes, and LLMs on the side of the code

daily-notes.nvim is a daily notes plugin for Neovim: one file per day, year/month folders, headers carried over from the previous day. doctr was a daemon that read git diffs and kept documentation in sync with an LLM.

Neither is an agent. Both are about not losing track of things, which is most of what mAGI's ledger and notes do now.

2026: agents in tmux

Most of the agent work is from this year.

  • January. multiclaude: several Claude Code instances working on features in parallel, each in a tmux window, coordinated by a supervisor. Plain Bash.

  • March. FlowPilot: browser automation that explores a site once with an agent, compiles scripts to replay it without LLM calls, and hands the live browser to a human over CDP when it hits a login or a CAPTCHA.

  • May. trie: an in-repo index of what each symbol does and why it changed, enforced at commit time and exposed to coding agents. Soren: a swarm of CLI agents, each in its own tmux window, with a shared mailbox, a router daemon, a health monitor and a journal. Its README says to keep your copy private because the memories and journals get personal.

  • November 4. bridge: you talk to one Claude Code session, by voice or text, and it runs the other agents in tmux. Speech-to-text and spoken replies run locally.

By bridge, the pieces were all there: one agent in front, workers in tmux windows, voice, a browser agents can drive. They were spread across repos and each needed setting up.

mAGI

mAGI puts them in one install. You log in and the orchestrator is already running in tmux. You speak or type to it. It starts other agents, operates the desktop through hyprctl, and asks you only for decisions.

Some parts map straight back:

  • The event bus delivers events to the orchestrator only when it is idle and its input box is empty (how it works). That's the AgentZero wishlist item about checking on a long task without interrupting it, from the other side.

  • The agent browser is a Chromium with DevTools on a local port, shared between you and the agent. FlowPilot's CDP handoff, without the Docker.

  • Probes in that browser can watch a messaging tab. The shipped example probe (off by default) is for WhatsApp, where Joy ran in 2022.

  • Daily notes are written by you and by the agent (0.3). daily-notes.nvim with a second author.

  • Voice and the orchestrator come from bridge.

The pattern I see: I keep building one thing to talk to, with other things doing the work behind it, and something that remembers what's still open. It moved from a chat app, to a product backend, to my own desktop.

When Project What it was

2022 dotfiles Neovim and terminal config
2023 Mavy (Mavex AI) One assistant, fourteen specialists behind a router
Jan 2024 AgentZero Minimal tool-calling agent
Feb 2024 PlanWeaver Plan-and-execute agent
Jul 2024 ChainFactory DSL for LLM pipelines, on PyPI
Jun 2025 daily-notes.nvim Daily notes in Neovim
Aug 2025 doctr Docs daemon driven by git diffs
Jan 2026 multiclaude Parallel Claude Code agents in tmux
Mar 2026 FlowPilot Browser automation with human handoff over CDP
May 2026 trie Index of meaning and intent for a codebase
May 2026 Soren Agent swarm in tmux with mailbox and journal
Nov 2026 bridge Talk to one Claude Code session; it runs the rest
Nov 2026 mAGI A Fedora/Hyprland setup built around LLM agents
