summary:
Building reusable code is one of the best ways to improve your productivity as a Flutter developer. Instead of rewriting the same logic, widgets, or utilities across multiple projects, you can extract them into a reusable package and share them with other developers.

Flutter makes this process straightforward through Dart packages and pub.dev, the official package ecosystem for Dart and Flutter.

In this guide, we'll walk through creating a Flutter package, structuring it properly, documenting it, testing it, and publishing it to pub.dev.

Whether you're building a reusable widget, helper utility, API client, or UI component library, this workflow will help you turn your code into a package that other developers can install and use.

1. Why create a Flutter package?

A Flutter package allows you to organize code into a reusable module that can be shared across multiple applications or published for the community.

For example, imagine you're working on multiple Flutter projects and keep writing the same things:

  • Custom buttons and reusable widgets
  • Form validation utilities
  • API handling logic
  • Date and currency formatters
  • Theme extensions
  • Animations
  • Networking helpers

Instead of copying and pasting this code from project to project, you can create a package once and maintain it in a single place.

Once published, other developers can install it with a simple dependency:

dependencies:
  my_package: ^1.0.0

That's the beauty of package development: write once, maintain once, and reuse everywhere.

2. Create your Flutter package

First, make sure Flutter is installed and working on your machine.

flutter doctor

Now create a new package using the Flutter CLI:

flutter create --template=package my_package

Navigate into the package directory:

cd my_package

Flutter generates the initial structure for you.

my_package/
├── lib/
│   ├── my_package.dart
│   └── src/
├── test/
│   └── my_package_test.dart
├── example/
├── pubspec.yaml
├── README.md
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── LICENSE
└── analysis_options.yaml

You don't need to create everything from scratch. The Flutter CLI gives you a starting point, so you can focus on the actual functionality of your package.

3. Understand the package structure

File / Directory Purpose
lib/ Public package code
lib/src/ Internal implementation
lib/my_package.dart Public API entry point
test/ Automated tests
example/ Example Flutter application
pubspec.yaml Package configuration and dependencies
README.md Documentation and usage instructions
CHANGELOG.md Version history
LICENSE License information

One important convention in Dart package development is keeping implementation files inside lib/src/ and exposing only the public API through your main package file.

This helps you maintain control over what consumers of your package can access.

4. Build your first reusable widget

Let's create something simple but useful — a reusable Flutter button.

Create a file inside lib/src/:

lib/src/custom_button.dart

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

class CustomButton extends StatelessWidget {
  final String text;
  final VoidCallback onPressed;
  final Color color;

  const CustomButton({
    super.key,
    required this.text,
    required this.onPressed,
    this.color = Colors.blue,
  });

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return ElevatedButton(
      onPressed: onPressed,
      style: ElevatedButton.styleFrom(
        backgroundColor: color,
        padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(
          horizontal: 24,
          vertical: 14,
        ),
      ),
      child: Text(text),
    );
  }
}

This widget accepts a label, callback, and optional color, making it reusable across different Flutter applications.

The important part isn't the button itself — it's how we're packaging and exposing the code.

5. Expose your public API

Open the main library file:

lib/my_package.dart

Export your widget:

library my_package;

export 'src/custom_button.dart';

This is the entry point for developers using your package.

Rather than importing internal files directly, consumers can now import everything through one clean interface:

import 'package:my_package/my_package.dart';

Keeping a clean public API is important. It allows you to change internal implementation later without breaking users who depend on your package.

6. Configure pubspec.yaml

The pubspec.yaml file is the heart of your package. It defines its name, version, description, SDK compatibility, dependencies, and other metadata.

name: my_package
description: A reusable Flutter button widget package.
version: 1.0.0
homepage: https://github.com/yourusername/my_package

environment:
  sdk: ^3.6.0
  flutter: ">=3.24.0"

dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter

dev_dependencies:
  flutter_test:
    sdk: flutter
  flutter_lints: ^5.0.0

A few things to keep in mind:

  • name — Your package name. It must be unique on pub.dev.
  • description — Clearly explain what your package does.
  • version — Follow semantic versioning.
  • environment — Define the Dart and Flutter versions your package supports.
  • dependencies — Add only what your package actually needs.
  • dev_dependencies — Tools used for testing, linting, and development.

Avoid adding unnecessary dependencies. A lightweight package is usually easier to install, maintain, and adopt.

7. Write tests before publishing

A package should not only work in your project — it should be reliable for other developers too.

Create a test inside test/ to verify your widget behaves as expected.

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart';
import 'package:my_package/my_package.dart';

void main() {
  testWidgets('CustomButton displays text', (tester) async {
    await tester.pumpWidget(
      MaterialApp(
        home: Scaffold(
          body: CustomButton(
            text: 'Click Me',
            onPressed: () {},
          ),
        ),
      ),
    );

    expect(find.text('Click Me'), findsOneWidget);
  });
}

Run your tests:

flutter test

If your package contains complex logic, add unit tests. If it contains widgets, add widget tests. Testing helps catch regressions before they reach users.

8. Create an example application

One of the most overlooked parts of package development is the example app.

A good example helps developers understand how your package works without having to read the entire source code.

Inside the example/ directory, you can demonstrate your package in a real Flutter application.

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:my_package/my_package.dart';

void main() {
  runApp(const ExampleApp());
}

class ExampleApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const ExampleApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      home: Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: const Text('My Package Example')),
        body: Center(
          child: CustomButton(
            text: 'Hello Package',
            onPressed: () {
              debugPrint('Button pressed!');
            },
          ),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Run the example app and make sure your package works exactly as expected.

cd example
flutter run

Your example app can also be a great place to showcase different configurations, edge cases, and use cases.

9. Documentation matters more than you think

Your package might have excellent code, but if developers don't understand how to use it, they probably won't use it.

A good README.md should include:

  • What your package does
  • Features
  • Installation instructions
  • Usage examples
  • API details
  • Screenshots or GIFs, if applicable
  • Supported platforms
  • Contribution guidelines

Documentation is not just an additional task. It's part of the product you're publishing.

10. Check your package before publishing

Before publishing, run the following commands from your package root.

Analyze your code 

flutter analyze

This checks for potential issues, warnings, and lint violations.

Run your tests 

flutter test

Check package quality 

dart pub publish --dry-run

This performs a validation pass and helps identify issues that could prevent your package from being published.

Take time to fix warnings, missing documentation, invalid metadata, and unnecessary files before proceeding.

11. Publish your package to pub.dev

Once everything is ready, you're finally at the publishing stage.

Make sure:

  • Your package name is available.
  • Your pubspec.yaml metadata is correct.
  • Your README is complete.
  • Tests are passing.
  • Your license is included.
  • Your Git repository is public if you're linking to it.

Then run:

dart pub publish

The Dart publishing workflow will guide you through the authentication and confirmation process if required.

Review the package contents and confirm publishing when prompted.

After successful publication, your package will be available on pub.dev.

You can share your package page with other developers, add it to your projects, and start receiving feedback.

12. Use your published package in another Flutter project

After publication, install it in any Flutter project by adding it to your dependencies.

flutter pub add my_package

Or manually add it to your pubspec.yaml:

dependencies:
  my_package: ^1.0.0

Then fetch the dependency:

flutter pub get

Import it:

import 'package:my_package/my_package.dart';

And start using it:

CustomButton(
  text: 'Continue',
  onPressed: () {
    debugPrint('Continue pressed');
  },
);

That's it. Your reusable code is now available through the Dart package ecosystem.

13. Maintain and update your package

Publishing version 1.0.0 isn't the end of package development. It's the beginning of maintaining it.

As developers use your package, you may need to fix bugs, add features, improve documentation, or support newer Flutter versions.

Follow semantic versioning:

Version change Meaning Example
Patch Bug fixes, backward-compatible changes 1.0.0 → 1.0.1
Minor New backward-compatible features 1.0.0 → 1.1.0
Major Breaking changes 1.0.0 → 2.0.0

Whenever you release an update:

  1. Update the version in pubspec.yaml.
  2. Add release notes to CHANGELOG.md.
  3. Run tests and analysis.
  4. Validate with dart pub publish --dry-run.
  5. Publish the new version using dart pub publish.

Good package maintenance builds trust. Developers are more likely to depend on packages that are documented, tested, and actively maintained.

Final thoughts

Creating and publishing a Flutter package is easier than it might seem. With the Flutter CLI, a clean project structure, proper testing, and good documentation, you can turn a small piece of reusable code into something that other developers can benefit from.

You don't need to build something huge to publish your first package. Start with a small utility, a useful widget, or a helper you already use in your projects.

The best packages often solve simple problems really well.

If you have code that you've reused more than once, maybe it's time to turn it into a package.

Build it. Document it. Test it. Publish it.

title: Open Ontologies 2.0: plan ontology changes before production
summary:
Open Ontologies 2.0

Approving a vocabulary mapping because the labels look right is not enough. Downstream, exactMatch means two terms are interchangeable, and a wrong match quietly changes what your data means. Open Ontologies plans ontology changes before they reach production. It reasons over each vocabulary separately and downgrades an exactMatch the evidence does not support, with the reason given. It also reports terms the mapping does not carry. It cannot confirm a match, and a wrong sibling under the right parent can still pass, so treat it as a check, not proof. As of 27 November 2026 it has 2,971 stars on GitHub, is MIT licensed, and the latest release is v2.1.0 from 23 October 2026.

Repo: https://github.com/fabio-rovai/open-ontologies

What you get

  • A plan for ontology changes before they reach production, with a blast radius report and a proof an auditor can re-check
  • Reasoning over each vocabulary separately, instead of trusting labels that look right
  • Unsupported exactMatch matches downgraded, with the reason given
  • A report of the terms a mapping does not carry

Treat it as a check, not proof: it can flag a bad match, but it cannot confirm a good one.

Quick poll

What would you use Open Ontologies 2.0 for first?

  • Planning an ontology change before production
  • Checking a vocabulary mapping for bad exactMatch
  • Reviewing terms a mapping does not carry
  • Reading the docs first

Vote in the comments.

If you found Open Ontologies 2.0 interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: Year-End Receipt Cleanup: 7 Steps I Run Before December (Plus 99 Free Templates I Just Open-Sourced)
summary:
Every November, the same posts start trending in freelancer communities: the year-end bookkeeping checklist. Chase the unpaid invoices. Log the last expenses. Back everything up.

And every year, step 3 is where it falls apart — the receipts.

They're in four inboxes, a downloads folder, and a glovebox. Some never existed on paper at all. So here is the cleanup I actually run, in the order that works, with the free tools for each step. No accounting suite required.

1. Match every payment to a document

Go through your bank/card statements for the year. Every business expense should have a matching receipt or invoice stored somewhere you can find it again in two years, not two minutes.

2. Recreate the simple ones yourself

For cash payments, small services and rent, you don't need the original till slip — you need a clean record of a real transaction. I generate these with Kitovo, a free receipt generator I built that runs entirely in the browser (no signup, nothing uploaded). Cash, rent, payment and service templates are all there.

3. Declare the genuinely lost ones — honestly

Some receipts are just gone. Most employers and tax processes accept a written missing-receipt declaration for a real purchase: what it was, when, how much, how you paid, signed and dated. What they don't accept is a fabricated receipt — and neither should you. There's a free missing receipt declaration generator for exactly this.

4. Log mileage and fuel properly

If you drive for work, fuel receipts and mileage are usually the biggest under-claimed pile. The rules differ by country, but the habit is the same: keep the receipt, log the trip. I wrote up the US side here: gas receipts for taxes.

5. Give every file a findable name

2026-03-14_supplier_59.99.pdf beats IMG_4021.jpg every time. Future you — and your accountant — will say thanks.

6. Export a full backup

Download a copy of everything: invoices issued, receipts, expense records. One cloud folder + one local copy. If a tool holds your records hostage behind a paywall, that's a sign to move before January, not after.

7. Start next year with templates, not panic

This is the part I just made easier — mostly for myself, but it's public now:

I open-sourced all 99 of Kitovo's blank receipt templates — 33 receipt types (rent, cash, freelance, donation, hotel, auto repair…), each in Word, Excel with live formulas, and fillable PDF:

→ https://github.com/codermillat/kitovo-free-receipt-templates

Star it, fork it, or just grab the one template you need. They're free for personal and commercial use, no attribution required.

The whole cleanup takes an afternoon if your records are decent, a weekend if they're not. Either way, December-you is much better placed to do it than February-you, reconstructing a year from bank statements.

What's your worst receipt gap at year-end — subscriptions, travel, or the cash payments nobody documented?
